5	// LEVEL 2 ("The Drone Bay") — a dispatch yard at scale.
6	//
7	// Twelve ship systems are dark out across the island, each at the end of its
8	// own track. You have only SIX subagent cars. You don't run — you DISPATCH,
9	// and because there are more jobs than cars, you reuse them:
10	//
11	//   drag a car onto a track     → it loads at the starting line
12	//   press SPACE                  → the green flag launches every loaded car
13	//   a track has a corruption patch → cars bog down in it and lose time
14	//   click a bogged car           → spend a nitro charge, it punches through
15	//   a car reaches its system      → its work seals (ice), the car drives home
16	//   re-dispatch the freed car      → onto the next open track
17	//   click a sealed job            → `entire checkpoint explain <id>` pre-filled
18	//   read what it did              → ADD TO SHIP (Y) → system online
19	//   all twelve online             → type `entire dispatch` — the day writes itself
20	//
21	// The clock is the rescue run: it starts on the green flag and stops the moment
22	// every job is sealed. Reviewing the work afterward is calm, untimed — but with
23	// twelve jobs, the review queue is real work. That friction is the lesson:
24	// you delegated it, so you owe every one of them a look before you accept it.
25	//
26	// The camera is a free mission-control eye: drag the background to orbit, scroll
27	// to zoom. Pull back for the whole yard, lean in to watch a car fight a patch.
28	
29	const TOTAL_TIME = 80;       // seconds for the rescue run (tunable)
30	const BASE_SPEED = 1 / 12;   // lane progress per second (clean lane ≈ 12s)
31	const RETURN_MULT = 2.4;     // freed cars hustle back to the bay
32	const BOOST_MULT = 2.6;      // nitro speed multiplier
33	const BOOST_DUR  = 2.2;      // seconds a nitro surge lasts
34	const NITRO_MAX  = 6;        // charges per run (tunable)
35	const HAZARD_SLOW = 0.30;    // speed multiplier inside a corruption patch
36	const HAZARD_FILL = 3.6;     // seconds in a severe patch before the car stalls
37	const STALL_CRAWL = 0.06;    // speed of a stalled car (basically stuck — boost it)
38	const LOW_TIME = 22;         // clock turns urgent under this
39	const CRIT_TIME = 10;        // clock goes CRITICAL under this
40	const PANIC_TIME = 28;       // the SKY starts shifting toward panic-red
41	const MELT_DUR = 1.2;        // seconds the ice takes to melt on ADD TO SHIP
42	
43	const N_CARS = 6;            // fewer cars than jobs — the reuse pressure
44	// The yard sits on a compact patch near the island centre so nothing lands in
45	// the sea (land is only reliable within ~radius 60 of centre).
46	// Tracks begin near the island's front edge (high +z) and run inward toward the
47	// high central ground where the systems sit. A narrower fan keeps the forward
48	// start line on solid land instead of the low shore.
49	const START_Z = 50;
50	const FINISH_Z = -12;
51	const LANE = (i, n) => ({ startX: (i - (n - 1) / 2) * 4, finishX: (i - (n - 1) / 2) * 5.5 });
52	// The dock sits OFF TO THE SIDE (a pier on the +x edge), up by the start line.
53	const DOCK_X = 40;
54	const DOCK_Z0 = 44;
55	const DOCK_DZ = -6;
56	const DOCK_CZ = DOCK_Z0 + (N_CARS - 1) * DOCK_DZ / 2;   // dock centre in z
57	const BAY_FACING = Math.PI / 2;                          // cars face -x, toward the tracks
58	const baySlot = (i) => ({ x: DOCK_X, z: DOCK_Z0 + i * DOCK_DZ });
59	const clamp = (v, a, b) => Math.max(a, Math.min(b, v));

221	// Per-lane corruption patch. Every third lane is severe (must be boosted);
222	// the rest just slow you. Staggered along the track so they don't all hit at once.
223	const HAZARDS = JOBS.map((_, i) => {
224	  const severe = i % 3 === 0;
225	  return { at: 0.30 + (i % 4) * 0.06, len: severe ? 0.18 : 0.10, severe };
226	});

320	function buildStarDome() {
321	  const g = new THREE.Group();
322	  const ped = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.9, 1.2, 1.2, 8), SCORCH());
323	  ped.position.y = 0.6;
324	  const stars = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
325	  const pts = new Float32Array(120 * 3);
326	  for (let i = 0; i < 120; i++) {
327	    const r = 1.2 + Math.random() * 1.4;
328	    const th = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;
329	    const ph = Math.random() * Math.PI * 0.5;
330	    pts[i * 3] = Math.cos(th) * Math.sin(ph) * r;
331	    pts[i * 3 + 1] = 3.2 + Math.cos(ph) * r * 0.9;
332	    pts[i * 3 + 2] = Math.sin(th) * Math.sin(ph) * r;
333	  }
334	  stars.setAttribute("position", new THREE.BufferAttribute(pts, 3));
335	  const field = new THREE.Points(stars, new THREE.PointsMaterial({
336	    color: 0xbfe9ff, size: 0.16, transparent: true, opacity: 0.95,
337	    blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending, depthWrite: false,
338	  }));

447	      color: 0xffb86b, transparent: true, opacity: 0, blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending, depthWrite: false,
448	    })
449	  );
450	  glow.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2;
451	  glow.position.y = 0.12;
452	  g.add(body, nose, cabin, glow);
453	  g.userData = { bodyMat, cabin, glow, wheels };
454	  return g;
455	}

457	// ---------- a volumetric corruption patch (reads at a low camera angle) ----------
458	function buildHazard(severe) {
459	  const g = new THREE.Group();
460	  const r = severe ? 3.4 : 2.2;
461	  const shardMat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
462	    color: 0x3a0a0a, emissive: 0xff3320, emissiveIntensity: 1.4, roughness: 0.5, metalness: 0.2,
463	  });
464	  const n = severe ? 7 : 5;
465	  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
466	    const h = (severe ? 2.6 : 1.6) * (0.6 + Math.random() * 0.7);
467	    const shard = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.ConeGeometry(0.5 + Math.random() * 0.4, h, 5), shardMat);
468	    const a = (i / n) * Math.PI * 2 + Math.random() * 0.4;
469	    const rad = Math.random() * r * 0.7;
470	    shard.position.set(Math.cos(a) * rad, h * 0.5, Math.sin(a) * rad);
471	    shard.rotation.set((Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.5, Math.random() * Math.PI, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.5);
472	    g.add(shard);
473	  }
474	  const domeMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
475	    color: 0xff5530, transparent: true, opacity: 0.18, side: THREE.DoubleSide,
476	    depthWrite: false, blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending,
477	  });
478	  const dome = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(r, 16, 10, 0, Math.PI * 2, 0, Math.PI / 2), domeMat);
479	  g.add(dome);
480	  const ringMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xffae66, transparent: true, opacity: 0.7 });
481	  const ring = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.TorusGeometry(r, 0.12, 8, 32), ringMat);
482	  ring.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2;
483	  ring.position.y = 0.15;
484	  g.add(ring);
485	  g.userData = { shardMat, domeMat, ringMat, severe, r };
486	  return g;
487	}

489	// The ship console behind the bay (decoration / where the report fires).
490	function makeConsole() {
491	  const g = new THREE.Group();
492	  const pedestal = new THREE.Mesh(
493	    new THREE.BoxGeometry(2.6, 4.6, 1.6),
494	    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x1c2230, metalness: 0.6, roughness: 0.35 })
495	  );
496	  pedestal.position.y = 2.3;
497	  const screen = new THREE.Mesh(
498	    new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2.1, 1.3),
499	    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
500	      color: 0x0c2030, emissive: 0x2a8aa6, emissiveIntensity: 1.4, roughness: 0.3,
501	    })
502	  );
503	  screen.position.set(0, 4.0, 0.82);
504	  screen.rotation.x = -0.28;
505	  g.add(pedestal, screen);
506	  return g;
507	}

509	export function createDroneBayView(renderer, { onExit, onComplete, onNext, onNewGame } = {}) {
510	  const canvas = renderer.domElement;
511	
512	  // ---------- scene & sky ----------
513	  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
514	  scene.background = SKY_CALM.clone();
515	  scene.fog = new THREE.Fog(SKY_CALM.clone(), 80, 190);
516	
517	  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(
518	    60, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 2000
519	  );
520	
521	  // ---------- mission-control camera (orbit + zoom around a target) ----------
522	  const camTarget = new THREE.Vector3(0, 1.5, 24);
523	  let camRadius = 52, camTheta = 0, camPhi = 1.2;
524	  function updateCamera() {
525	    const sinPhi = Math.sin(camPhi);
526	    camera.position.set(
527	      camTarget.x + camRadius * sinPhi * Math.sin(camTheta),
528	      camTarget.y + camRadius * Math.cos(camPhi),
529	      camTarget.z + camRadius * sinPhi * Math.cos(camTheta)
530	    );
531	    camera.lookAt(camTarget);
532	  }
533	  updateCamera();
534	
535	  // ---------- lighting ----------
536	  scene.add(new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xcdbcff, 0x3a2f5e, 0.7));
537	  const sun = new THREE.DirectionalLight(SUN_CALM, 1.5);
538	  sun.position.set(60, 90, 40);
539	  scene.add(sun);
540	  scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0x6a5a92, 0.3));
541	
542	  const dome = new THREE.Mesh(
543	    new THREE.SphereGeometry(900, 32, 16),
544	    new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: DOME_CALM.clone(), side: THREE.BackSide, fog: false })
545	  );
546	  scene.add(dome);
547	
548	  // ---------- terrain (the same island) ----------
549	  const terrain = createTerrain({ size: 200, segments: 220, maxHeight: 26, seed: 1337 });
550	  scene.add(terrain.mesh, terrain.water);
551	
552	  const beamTex = makeBeamTexture();
553	
554	  const BUILD = {
555	    buildBrokenCoils, buildBrokenNav, buildBrokenDish, buildBrokenVent, buildBrokenStrut,
556	    buildPlasmaRing, buildStarDome, buildGardenPod, buildGravSkid,
557	    buildSignalSpire: () => buildSignalSpire(beamTex),
558	  };
559	
560	  function railGeo(a, b, offX, terr) {
561	    const NP = 24;
562	    const pts = [];
563	    for (let i = 0; i <= NP; i++) {
564	      const k = i / NP;
565	      const x = a.x + (b.x - a.x) * k + offX;
566	      const z = a.z + (b.z - a.z) * k;
567	      pts.push(new THREE.Vector3(x, terr.heightAt(x, z) + 0.25, z));
568	    }
569	    return new THREE.BufferGeometry().setFromPoints(pts);
570	  }
571	
572	  // ---------- the twelve lanes ----------
573	  const N = JOBS.length;
574	  const lanes = JOBS.map((data, idx) => {
575	    const { startX, finishX } = LANE(idx, N);
576	    const start = new THREE.Vector3(startX, terrain.heightAt(startX, START_Z) + 0.6, START_Z);
577	    const finish = new THREE.Vector3(finishX, terrain.heightAt(finishX, FINISH_Z), FINISH_Z);
578	    const hazard = HAZARDS[idx];
579	
580	    const anchor = new THREE.Group();
581	    anchor.position.copy(finish);
582	    const brokenModel = BUILD[data.broken]();
583	    const upgradeModel = BUILD[data.upgrade]();
584	    upgradeModel.visible = false;
585	    anchor.add(brokenModel, upgradeModel);
586	
587	    // Status beam — taller and brighter so it reads from across the yard.
588	    const beam = new THREE.Mesh(
589	      new THREE.CylinderGeometry(1.0, 1.0, 80, 12, 1, true),
590	      new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
591	        map: beamTex, color: 0xff8a5c, transparent: true, opacity: 0.34,
592	        blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending, depthWrite: false, side: THREE.DoubleSide, fog: false,
593	      })
594	    );
595	    beam.position.y = 46;
596	    anchor.add(beam);
597	
598	    const ice = makeIceBlock();
599	    ice.scale.setScalar(1.25);
600	    ice.position.y = 2.6;
601	    ice.visible = false;
602	    anchor.add(ice);
603	    const sprite = makeIdSprite(data.ckpt);
604	    sprite.position.y = 8.4;
605	    sprite.visible = false;
606	    anchor.add(sprite);
607	
608	    // Invisible click target for reviewing a sealed job (the car drives off).
609	    const reviewHit = new THREE.Mesh(
610	      new THREE.BoxGeometry(7, 9, 7),
611	      new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ transparent: true, opacity: 0, depthWrite: false })
612	    );
613	    reviewHit.position.y = 3.5;
614	    reviewHit.userData.reviewLaneIdx = idx;
615	    anchor.add(reviewHit);
616	    scene.add(anchor);
617	
618	    const railMat = new THREE.LineBasicMaterial({ color: 0x35506a, transparent: true, opacity: 0.6 });
619	    const railL = new THREE.Line(railGeo(start, finish, -1.2, terrain), railMat);
620	    const railR = new THREE.Line(railGeo(start, finish, 1.2, terrain), railMat);
621	    scene.add(railL, railR);
622	
623	    const hzFrac = hazard.at + hazard.len / 2;
624	    const hx = start.x + (finish.x - start.x) * hzFrac;
625	    const hzz = start.z + (finish.z - start.z) * hzFrac;
626	    const hzMesh = buildHazard(hazard.severe);
627	    hzMesh.position.set(hx, terrain.heightAt(hx, hzz) + 0.3, hzz);
628	    scene.add(hzMesh);
629	
630	    return {
631	      data, idx, start, finish, hazard, anchor, brokenModel, upgradeModel, beam, ice, sprite,
632	      reviewHit, railL, railR, railMat, hzMesh,
633	      carObj: null,
634	      state: "empty",          // empty → loaded → running → sealed → added
635	      prog: 0, boostT: 0, corrupt: 0, meltT: 0,
636	      stalled: false, hazardCleared: false,
637	    };
638	  });
639	
640	  // ---------- the dock: a built pier off to the side where the cars wait ----------
641	  // One deck height for the whole platform so cars sit flush on it.
642	  let deckY = -Infinity;
643	  for (let i = 0; i < N_CARS; i++) { const s = baySlot(i); deckY = Math.max(deckY, terrain.heightAt(s.x, s.z)); }
644	  deckY += 0.5;
645	
646	  // ---------- the car pool (parked on the dock) ----------
647	  const cars = Array.from({ length: N_CARS }, (_, i) => {
648	    const mesh = buildCar();
649	    const s = baySlot(i);
650	    const home = new THREE.Vector3(s.x, deckY + 0.35, s.z);
651	    mesh.position.copy(home);
652	    mesh.rotation.y = BAY_FACING;
653	    mesh.userData.carIdx = i;
654	    scene.add(mesh);
655	    return {
656	      mesh, home, idx: i, state: "bay", lane: null,    // bay → loaded → running → returning → bay
657	      retProg: 0, retFrom: null, retTo: null,
658	    };
659	  });
660	
661	  // The pier itself: a long deck on stilts down the +x edge, glowing rim.
662	  const dockW = 10;                                        // narrow in x
663	  const dockD = Math.abs((N_CARS - 1) * DOCK_DZ) + 12;     // the column + margin
664	  {
665	    const dock = new THREE.Group();
666	    const deck = new THREE.Mesh(
667	      new THREE.BoxGeometry(dockW, 0.5, dockD),
668	      new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2a2230, metalness: 0.5, roughness: 0.6 })
669	    );
670	    deck.position.set(DOCK_X, deckY - 0.25, DOCK_CZ);
671	    dock.add(deck);
672	    const edge = new THREE.Mesh(
673	      new THREE.BoxGeometry(dockW + 0.4, 0.14, dockD + 0.4),
674	      new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x6fe3ff, transparent: true, opacity: 0.5 })
675	    );
676	    edge.position.set(DOCK_X, deckY + 0.02, DOCK_CZ);
677	    dock.add(edge);
678	    const postMat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x171019, metalness: 0.4, roughness: 0.75 });
679	    for (const sx of [-1, 1]) for (const sz of [-1, 1]) {
680	      const px = DOCK_X + sx * (dockW / 2 - 1.2), pz = DOCK_CZ + sz * (dockD / 2 - 1.2);
681	      const gy = terrain.heightAt(px, pz);
682	      const ph = Math.max(0.6, deckY - 0.5 - gy);
683	      const post = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.5, 0.5, ph, 8), postMat);
684	      post.position.set(px, gy + ph / 2, pz);
685	      dock.add(post);
686	    }
687	    scene.add(dock);
688	  }
689	
690	  // ---------- the ship console (behind the start line) ----------
691	  const consoleAnchor = new THREE.Group();
692	  const cz = START_Z + 14;
693	  consoleAnchor.position.set(0, terrain.heightAt(0, cz), cz);
694	  consoleAnchor.add(makeConsole());
695	  const consoleGlow = new THREE.PointLight(0xffd27a, 5, 28, 2);
696	  consoleGlow.position.y = 5;

767	  const allAdded = () => addedCount() >= lanes.length;
768	  const loadedCount = () => lanes.filter((l) => l.state === "loaded").length;

775	  // ---------- raycasting / pointer ----------
776	  const raycaster = new THREE.Raycaster();
777	  const ndc = new THREE.Vector2();
778	  const groundPlane = new THREE.Plane(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0), 0);
779	  let hoverCar = null;
780	  let pointerDown = false;

782	  let pickedJob = null;         // sealed job under the cursor at mousedown
783	  let pickedKind = null;        // "car" | "job" | "camera"

789	  function setNdc(e) {
790	    const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
791	    ndc.x = ((e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width) * 2 - 1;
792	    ndc.y = -((e.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height) * 2 + 1;
793	  }
794	  function carAtPointer(e) {
795	    setNdc(e);
796	    raycaster.setFromCamera(ndc, camera);
797	    const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects(cars.map((c) => c.mesh), true);
798	    if (!hits.length) return null;
799	    let o = hits[0].object;
800	    while (o && o.userData.carIdx === undefined) o = o.parent;
801	    return o ? cars[o.userData.carIdx] : null;
802	  }
803	  function jobAtPointer(e) {
804	    setNdc(e);
805	    raycaster.setFromCamera(ndc, camera);
806	    const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects(lanes.map((l) => l.reviewHit));
807	    if (!hits.length) return null;
808	    const l = lanes[hits[0].object.userData.reviewLaneIdx];
809	    return l && l.state === "sealed" ? l : null;
810	  }
811	  function groundAt(e) {
812	    setNdc(e);
813	    raycaster.setFromCamera(ndc, camera);
814	    const p = new THREE.Vector3();
815	    return raycaster.ray.intersectPlane(groundPlane, p) ? p : null;
816	  }
817	  function nearestEmptyLane(p) {
818	    if (!p) return null;
819	    let best = null, bd = 1e9;
820	    for (const l of lanes) {
821	      if (l.state !== "empty") continue;
822	      const d = Math.hypot(p.x - l.start.x, p.z - l.start.z);
823	      if (d < bd) { bd = d; best = l; }
824	    }
825	    return (best && bd < 9) ? best : null;
826	  }

884	  function fmtTime(s) {

891	    countdownEl?.classList.toggle("is-critical", timerRunning && timeLeft <= CRIT_TIME);
892	  }
893	  function panicFactor() {
894	    if (failed) return 1;
895	    if (!timerRunning || timeLeft > PANIC_TIME) return 0;
896	    let p = (PANIC_TIME - timeLeft) / PANIC_TIME;
897	    p *= p;
898	    if (timeLeft <= CRIT_TIME) {
899	      const throb = 0.5 + 0.5 * Math.sin(performance.now() / 85);
900	      p += 0.14 * throb;
901	    }
902	    return Math.min(1, p);
903	  }

10	Agreed with Rizel 2026-06-10, replacing the built Archive level (shelved, kept in `src/archiveView.js`, playable at `?view=archive`). BUILT 2026-06-10 in `src/droneBayView.js` (#db-hud markup, post-L1 pin + ?view=level2 route here now); 150s clock, 18s drone work time, both tunable. Drones IMPROVISE (Rizel's "bow turns into a sword"): coils→Plasma Ring, nav core→Star Dome, dish→Signal Spire, scrubbers→Garden Pod, struts→Grav Skid — the transformation creates the "what did you DO?" urge that explain satisfies. Beam-color status grammar: amber broken → cyan working → ice-blue review-me → none (upgrade is the landmark). Ground levels in the day-to-day agentic workflow: **delegate → review → accept**. Level 2 "The Drone Bay": 5 broken ship systems (ignition coils, nav core, antenna, life support, landing struts), 5 drones (one per job, no economy). Assign with E (drone flies out and works); player chooses serial vs. parallel — the one countdown makes parallel the rational move. Finished sites seal under a checkpoint; walk up → terminal opens **pre-filled** with `entire checkpoint explain <id>` (Rizel: never type ids) → Enter → story card of what the drone did → **ADD TO SHIP** confirm (Y) → meter +20%. Finish line (changed 2026-06-10): the FIFTH accept keeps the terminal open and you type `entire dispatch` right there — the day's report writes itself from the checkpoints ("Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" per the real CLI). Rizel couldn't find the end-of-level console ("where am I supposed to be going") → no final fetch-quest; next command at the prompt you're already at. `entire checkpoint list` still accepted as an optional L1 callback. Bird's-eye map (M, src/overhead.js) added to all island levels; terminals stay open over it. Deliberately excluded: botched-drone deduction puzzles, drone management, extracting values from explanations (Rizel rejected those as "too complicated"). Teaching — use Rizel's framing (2026-06-10), not workflow jargon like "delegate→review→accept": the level shows **multiple agents working in parallel, seeing what work each did (explain), and getting a summary at the end (dispatch)**. Sending a drone is one button (spectacle, not a lesson); ADD TO SHIP is just the gate that makes reading the explanation non-skippable. Terminology (Rizel, 2026-06-10): in all player-facing copy the workers are called **subagents**, never drones — only the location keeps the name "The Drone Bay" (possible later rename; candidates discussed: The Fleet, Mission Control, fiction-patch "drones piloted by subagents"). Why: the word should make the real-world mapping unmistakable — these are agents working in parallel (or sequentially, player's choice) and you get insight into their work. Not metaphor decoration. See [[level2-archive-search-design]] and [[level2-design-direction]].

12	**REWORKED 2026-06-16 — starting-grid / mission-control rebuild.** Rizel disliked walking the island to scattered sites; redesigned the dispatch layer (NOT the explain/dispatch teaching, which is unchanged) into a fixed-camera racing-grid. droneBayView.js rewritten: dropped first-person (firstPerson.js), overhead map (overhead.js), pointer-lock, walk-up proximity, and the E-assign key. Now: fixed camera over 5 parallel lanes; subagents are **cars** (not drones) parked on a grid, rails drawn along terrain. **Click a car = arm; Space = green flag (launches all armed at once); click a moving car = nitro boost.** This one mechanic gives both sequential (arm-one-then-Space) and parallel (arm all five) — Rizel explicitly wanted both. Nitro = the engagement-during-travel + catch-up tool (3 charges/run, shown as dots in #db-systems-rows); Rizel didn't care what "powerups" meant, "just something where they go faster." Lanes are LOCAL to L2 (props placed at lane-ends, START_Z=64→FINISH_Z=-34, slight fan) and decoupled from SYSTEMS.pos — left SYSTEMS.pos untouched because launchView.js (L3) still reads it for its own island. Tunables: BASE_SPEED 1/14, BOOST_MULT 2.6, BOOST_DUR 2.2, NITRO_MAX 3, TOTAL_TIME 150. Kept: clock+panic sky, checkpoint cards, click-sealed-car→pre-filled explain→ADD TO SHIP→dispatch finish, win/fail. Open/untested live: car speed feel, whether any lane-end finish lands in water. Briefing + CONTROLS in index.html (#db-briefing) rewritten to match (click/Space, no WASD/E/M).

14	**TENSION REBUILD 2026-06-16 — dispatch grid (drag + generic hazards).** Playtest of the starting-grid version: "kinda good but no tension." Diagnosed: cars were already on rails (just flipping a switch), clock far too generous (150s vs ~14s parallel), nitro had no job, parallel overlap means the slowest lane sets finish time so an aggregate clock CAN'T create parallel tension (mathematically — boosting only the slowest barely helps). Conclusion: parallel "chaos" tension MUST come from a per-lane failure stake, not the clock. Agreed direction with Rizel: **true drag + generic hazards** (rejected specialty-matching cars/Decoder/Repair — it's the "drone management" she already killed, blows the 15s onboarding, and telegraphs outcomes which guts the explain payoff). Built in droneBayView.js: cars now wait in a BAY (BAY_Z=START_Z+26=90), tracks start EMPTY. Verbs: **drag** a car bay→track (loads at line), **Space** green-flags all loaded, **click** a bogged running car to nitro through. Decoupled car pool (`cars[]`, state bay→loaded→running→done) from `lanes[]` (state empty→loaded→running→sealed→added); lane.carObj links them. Drag = mousedown/mousemove(>5px)/mouseup, ground-plane raycast for position, nearestEmptyLane (|Δx|<9 & z<BAY_Z-10) for drop; click vs drag disambiguated by movement. Each lane has a corruption patch (HAZARDS[]: 2 severe + 3 mild, staggered): inside, speed×HAZARD_SLOW(0.30); SEVERE lanes also fill `corrupt` over HAZARD_FILL(3.6s) → STALL (crawl at STALL_CRAWL 0.06, basically stuck) unless boosted; boost (nitro--) clears the patch + un-stalls. NITRO_MAX=3 < 5 cars = the triage choice (cover the 2 severe). **Clock is now the RESCUE RUN**: starts on first green flag (clockStarted), stops the moment allHome() (every lane sealed/added) — so reviewing explanations is calm/untimed (protects the lesson). TOTAL_TIME=50, BASE_SPEED=1/12, LOW_TIME=18/CRIT=8/PANIC=22 — all tunable, NOT yet playtested. Fail modes that create tension: sequential bleeds the clock, a car left in the bay never homes (clock kills you), wasting nitro on mild lanes → severe stalls → fail. Hazard discs (buildHazard) sit on tracks so you can read severity before launch; drop-target lane rails brighten cyan while dragging; is-stalled CSS row = red blink "BOGGED". Briefing/controls rewritten again (drag/Space/click). Rizel will feel-out & tune the constants (she did this for L1 timer).

Key design calls she made in discussion: **Level 3 stays FROZEN** (the 5 hero SYSTEMS untouched, still exported for L3); **explain+ADD TO SHIP stays REQUIRED on all 12** — she explicitly said the review IS the friction/lesson and chose "all twelve required, reading-fatigue be damned" (I'd argued dosage matters / required×12 = rubber-stamp; she overrode, fine — feel it in play). Built: `JOBS = [...SYSTEMS(5 hero), ...GENERIC_JOBS(7)]` = 12 tracks; generic jobs are L2-only (own ckpts/cards, reuse the 5 broken+5 upgrade prop builders, never seen by L3). 6 cars (N_CARS) < 12 jobs → **reuse loop**: car seals its job → detaches (lane.carObj=null, lane stays "sealed" for review) → car.state="returning" drives itself back to its home bay slot (RETURN_MULT 2.4) → "bay" → re-draggable. Review now triggers by **clicking the sealed JOB** (invisible reviewHit box at the anchor, jobAtPointer raycast) since the car has driven off — not by clicking the car. **Free mission-control camera**: orbit (drag empty background) + zoom (scroll wheel); spherical around camTarget(0,0,14), camRadius 56-210, camPhi 0.5-1.45, camTheta ±0.9. Side panel can't show 12 rows → **aggregate tally** (db-jobs/db-tally CSS): "online x/12", en route / to review / bogged counts, cars free n/6. Built a real DOCK, then moved it OFF TO THE SIDE (Rizel: dock to the side, view should start on the tracks). Dock is now a pier on the +x edge: DOCK_X=46, cars in a z-column (DOCK_Z0=24, DOCK_DZ=-6, 6 slots z 24..-6), baySlot(i)={x:46,z:24-6i}, deck box (narrow x=10, long z) on 4 stilts + cyan rim, cars parked ON deck (home.y=deckY+0.35) facing -x (BAY_FACING=π/2, nose→-x toward the field). nearestEmptyLane now distance-to-start-point (hypot<9), geometry-agnostic so side-dock drops work. Then (Rizel: tracks should START near the beginning/front edge of the island + more zoom): pushed the whole field FORWARD toward the +z shore and NARROWED the fan so the forward outer lanes stay on land — START_Z=50, FINISH_Z=-12, LANE startX*4 finishX*5.5 (the island's high ground is central; the front is low shore, so a wide forward fan hits water — narrowing was the fix). Dock moved up alongside: DOCK_X=40, DOCK_Z0=44. Verified via /tmp/landcheck.mjs sweeping candidates: chosen layout "H" has min heights beam 3.3 / start 3.7 / track 3.3 / dock 2.2 (all on land). Camera zoomed in + front-biased: camTarget(0,1.5,24), camRadius 52 (zoom 36-150), camPhi 1.2, theta 0 — opens at the start of the tracks looking inward, dock at right. clamps theta ±0.8 / phi 0.72-1.36. NOTE the 12-lane WIDTH is the recurring constraint on both forward placement (outer lanes → water) and zoom (outer lanes → off-screen); narrowing the fan bought room but fewer lanes would buy more. KEY TRICK for "no water": tightened fog to 80-190 so the distant sea hazes into the sky colour instead of trying to win the geometry fight (you can't both hide water AND avoid bird's-eye on a round island — fog resolves it). > AGENT

I've read the whole current Level 2 (the uncommitted "dispatch yard" rebuild — 12 jobs / 6 cars) plus the full design history. Dev server is running at **http://localhost:5174/?view=level2** if you want to play along while we talk.

Here's my honest read. The *lesson* layer (improvise → `explain` → `dispatch`) is solid and worth protecting. The *dispatch game* around it is where I see problems — and notably it's been rebuilt four times, so you already feel that too.

## The two things I'd flag hardest

**1. The level splits into two phases that don't reinforce each other.**
- Phase 1 (timed): drag → Space → nitro. Pure logistics. Has nothing to do with checkpoints.
- Phase 2 (untimed): click sealed job → Enter → read → Y, **twelve times**. This is the actual lesson — and it's the chore at the end.

The fun mechanic and the teaching mechanic are bolted together but don't feed each other. A player can enjoy the cars and then rubber-stamp Enter/Y twelve times through structurally identical cards ("X broke → became Y"). That's the exact "required×12 = rubber-stamp" risk you overrode on 2026-06-10 — and you said you'd feel it in play. Having now read it cold: I think you'll feel it. Twelve reads of the same card shape teaches players to *stop reading*, which inverts the whole point of `explain`.

**2. The triage pressure the design wants isn't in the numbers.**
`NITRO_MAX = 6`, and severe lanes are `i % 3 === 0` → indices 0/3/6/9 = **4 severe lanes**. 6 charges ≥ 4 severe means you can nitro every severe lane *and* have 2 to spare. The "spend nitro wisely or a lane stalls and you fail" choice doesn't exist right now. Your earlier drag+hazards version had `NITRO 3 < 5 cars` precisely for this — the scale rebuild lost the scarcity.

## Smaller things
- **Review queue is a scavenger hunt.** The 12 rows don't fit, so the HUD shows counts only — to review the next job you orbit the camera hunting for an ice-blue beam among 12 lanes. Friction stacked on top of the 12× grind.
- **Drag fatigue:** 12 jobs / 6 cars = minimum 12 one-at-a-time drags + camera orbits per run. Feels like busywork more than strategy.
- **Onboarding copy still pending** (your own note) — and the current `BRIEFING_BEATS` are 3 beats with em-dashes, but you wanted 2 load-bearing beats, no em-dashes.

## My recommendation
The clock and nitro are just knobs — easy. The real fork is **the 12-job decision**. My instinct: the scale rebuild traded the soul (savoring each "wait, what did it DO?" transformation) for a multitasking *feel*, and the cost lands squarely on the lesson. I'd pull the count back down (≈6 jobs / 3 cars — still one reuse wave, still parallel, but a review queue you can actually savor), and spend the saved complexity making `explain` *load-bearing* during play rather than a tax after it.

But that reopens a call you already made, so I want your steer before I touch anything.

That's the real signal — thank you. It reframes everything: the current design deliberately **stops the clock for review** ("protect the lesson"), but you want the exact opposite — clearing the queue with `entire explain` *is* the frantic timed game. Today explain is the calm tax after the fun; you want explain to **be** the fun.

And the "doesn't remind me of any game" part is the giveaway: the cars-on-tracks dispatch isn't a recognizable loop. L1 has a clear genre (shooter). L2 needs one too.

So the fix isn't tuning — it's picking a known frantic-juggling game to build the *review rush* on, where the 12 finished jobs pile up and you race to `explain` + ship them before time's out. Here are three skins I'd consider. Pick the vibe and I'll redesign around it.

Locked in: **Overcooked order-ticket rush.** Here's the concrete design before I rewrite the view — tell me if this matches the picture in your head.

## The new Level 2 view

**No more island/cars/lanes/drag/nitro/hazards/free-camera.** Fixed camera at the ship's **command pass** — you never move. That alone fixes "the view."

**The loop:**
1. Press Space → the shift starts. Your 6 subagents start working in parallel in the background (a row of them busy behind the pass — that's the "parallel work" the level teaches, now shown as a flurry, not a logistics chore).
2. Finished jobs ride in toward you on a **conveyor / pass rail** as glowing checkpoint slates — and the improvised upgrade sits *on* the slate (the plasma ring, star dome, etc.), so you still get the "wait, what did it DO?" hook the level lives on. Slate shows system name + short ckpt id, sealed in ice-blue.
3. **Click a slate → `entire checkpoint explain` flips it** to the card (what the subagent actually did) — your existing DOM card. **Y / swipe → ADD TO SHIP.** The slate flies off to the ship, a hull light comes on, next ticket slides up.
4. All 12 online → the pass clears and you type **`entire dispatch`** right there — the report writes itself. Win.

**The reversal you asked for:** the clock runs *the whole time* now. Explain isn't the calm tax at the end — clearing the rail with explain **is** the timed game. Tickets keep arriving; that's the "omg can I keep up."

**Kept / frozen:** the 5 hero SYSTEMS (still exported for L3, untouched), the 7 generics, all the cards, the explain→ADD→dispatch terminal flow, beam/ice/ckpt-sprite + upgrade-model props, panic sky, win/fail screens. **Cut:** firstPerson/overhead are already unused; I'd also drop the cars/lanes/dock/hazard/nitro code.

You're right — that mechanic lies about the fiction. Food goes cold and customers walk; a checkpoint is a permanent record, and `explain` works on it forever. Borrowing "the order expires" would be a tell that we cargo-culted Overcooked instead of fitting it to what's actually true here.

So: **drop per-ticket expiry entirely.** Nothing you can do makes a record unreviewable. The honest pressure is the **launch window** — the ship is trying to leave, and a system isn't *online* until you've looked at it (`explain`) and added it. The subagents finish faster than you can review, so the rail floods. The "omg" is the closing clock against a growing pile, not rotting tickets.

  "content": "import fs from \"fs\";\n\nconst base = \"http://localhost:9222\";\nconst targets = await (await fetch(`${base}/json/list`)).json();\nconst page = targets.find((t) => t.type === \"page\" && t.url.includes(\"view=level2\")) || targets.find((t) => t.type === \"page\");\nif (!page) { console.error(\"no page target\", targets.map(t=>t.url)); process.exit(1); }\nconst ws = new WebSocket(page.webSocketDebuggerUrl);\nlet id = 0;\nconst pending = new Map();\nconst errors = [];\nfunction send(method, params = {}) {\n  return new Promise((res) => { const i = ++id; pending.set(i, res); ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id: i, method, params })); });\n}\nws.addEventListener(\"message\", (ev) => {\n  const m = JSON.parse(ev.data);\n  if (m.id && pending.has(m.id)) { pending.get(m.id)(m.result); pending.delete(m.id); }\n  else if (m.method === \"Runtime.exceptionThrown\") errors.push(m.params.exceptionDetails.exception?.description || m.params.exceptionDetails.text);\n  else if (m.method === \"Runtime.consoleAPICalled\" && m.params.type === \"error\") errors.push(\"console.error: \" + m.params.args.map(a=>a.value).join(\" \"));\n});\nawait new Promise((r) => ws.addEventListener(\"open\", r));\nawait send(\"Page.enable\");\nawait send(\"Runtime.enable\");\n\nconst sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));\nasync function key(code, k, vk) {\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchKeyEvent\", { type: \"keyDown\", code, key: k, windowsVirtualKeyCode: vk, nativeVirtualKeyCode: vk });\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchKeyEvent\", { type: \"keyUp\", code, key: k, windowsVirtualKeyCode: vk, nativeVirtualKeyCode: vk });\n}\nasync function click(x, y) {\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchMouseEvent\", { type: \"mousePressed\", x, y, button: \"left\", clickCount: 1 });\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchMouseEvent\", { type: \"mouseReleased\", x, y, button: \"left\", clickCount: 1 });\n}\nasync function shot(path) {\n  const { data } = await send(\"Page.captureScreenshot\", { format: \"png\" });\n  fs.writeFileSync(path, Buffer.from(data, \"base64\"));\n}\n\nawait sleep(500);\nawait key(\"Space\", \" \", 32);   // beat 1 -> 2\nawait sleep(300);\nawait key(\"Space\", \" \", 32);   // begin\nawait sleep(9000);             // let subagents finish, pass floods\nawait shot(\"/tmp/l2_mid.png\");\n// sweep clicks across the pass band to hit a front slate -> explain\nfor (const x of [240, 430, 620, 810, 1000]) { await click(x, 430); await sleep(120); }\nawait sleep(400);\nawait shot(\"/tmp/l2_explain.png\");\nawait key(\"KeyY\", \"y\", 89);    // ADD TO SHIP the focused\nawait sleep(700);\nawait shot(\"/tmp/l2_added.png\");\n\nconsole.log(\"EXCEPTIONS:\", errors.length ? errors : \"none\");\nws.close();\n"
}

Loop: Space×2 briefing (now 2 load-bearing beats, no em-dashes) → all 6 subagents wake; round-robin 2 jobs each (WORK_TIME 6.5 ±2.5 jitter) → finished job pushed to `pass[]`, slate slides in from ENTRANCE_X to its slot (VISIBLE_SLOTS=5, SLOT_X0 -16 / SLOT_DX 8; extras back up off-screen but still count). **Click slate = run explain** (focuses + flips, card in repurposed #terminal as a NON-blocking panel — pointer stays live so the pass keeps flooding while you read); **Y or ADD TO SHIP button** = added → slate flies to its hull pip, ice melts, pip greens. Done — Level 2 is rebuilt as the **Overcooked command-pass rush** and verified rendering + playing through the full loop with zero errors. It's live at **http://localhost:5174/?view=level2** — go feel it out.

**What changed**
- Ripped out the cars/lanes/drag/nitro/hazards/dock/free-camera (and the island terrain). Replaced with a **fixed command pass**: six subagents working behind you, a scrolling belt, a 12-pip ship hull board at the back.
- Finished jobs **ride up the pass as checkpoint slates**, each carrying its improvised upgrade under ice — the "what did it DO?" reveal survives.
- **Click a slate → `entire checkpoint explain` runs** (card opens as a *non-blocking* panel, so the pass keeps flooding while you read) → **Y / ADD TO SHIP** → it flies to the hull, the pip goes green, the next ticket slides in.
- **The launch clock now runs the whole time and drains faster the bigger your unreviewed pile** ("ship unstable") — clearing the queue with `explain` *is* the timed game, which is the flip you asked for. Nothing expires (your point — the record is permanent).
- All 12 online → type `entire dispatch` → win. Briefing is now 2 load-bearing beats, no em-dashes.
- Level 3 is untouched (still imports `SYSTEMS`/`UPGRADE_BUILDERS`).

**Knobs to feel out** (top of `droneBayView.js`, like you tuned the L1 timer): `TOTAL_TIME 75`, `WORK_TIME 6.5` (±`2.5`), `RAIL_DRAIN 0.14` (how hard the backlog bites), `VISIBLE_SLOTS 5`, `BACKLOG_PANIC 5`.

**Two things I noticed in the screenshots, your call:**
1. Slates are big and a touch cramped at `SLOT_DX 8` — easy to widen or shrink them.
2. The non-blocking review panel could use a visible tie-line to the focused slate so it's obvious which one you're reading.

It's all uncommitted (same as how you've been iterating) — I didn't commit. Want me to tune any of those knobs, or do you want to play it first?

> AGENT

Done. The **delegate step is back** — Level 2 now opens with you sending the crew out before the review rush.

**How it plays now:**
1. Briefing (2 beats) → the six subagents sit idle, each flagged **SEND ▸** with a pulsing ring. The launch clock is **paused**.
2. **Click a subagent to send it out** — or **Space to dispatch the whole crew**. You can stagger (send a few now, the rest later = your parallel-vs-sequential call).
3. The clock starts on your **first** dispatch — so the delegate beat is deliberate, not rushed.
4. Each dispatched subagent auto-takes its second job, so you're not micromanaging — the rush stays about `explain`. Finished jobs ride up the pass → click = explain → Y = add to ship.

Verified headlessly through the whole chain (briefing → dispatch → clock starts → flood → explain → add) with zero runtime exceptions. Dev server's still up at **http://localhost:5174/?view=level2** — give it a play.

One thing worth a thought once you've felt it: right now subagents **auto-take their second job**, so you dispatch once at the start and never again. If you want the delegation to *recur* (re-send each one for its second job while you're also reviewing), that's the "ongoing tasking" variant — say the word and I'll switch it. Otherwise this keeps the send as a clean opening step.

42 : w.phase === \"work\" ? 26 : 0;\n        for (const r of ud.rotors) r.rotation.y += spin * dt;\n        // gentle hover bob/tilt on the craft body\n        ud.craft.position.y = 2.6 + Math.sin((t + w.home.x) * 2.2) * 0.12;\n\n        if (!w.dispatched) {\n          const pulse = 0.5 + 0.5 * Math.sin(t * 4 + w.home.x);\n          ud.ring.material.opacity = 0.45 + pulse * 0.45;\n          ud.ring.scale.setScalar(1 + pulse * 0.06);\n          ud.eyeMat.emissiveIntensity = 0.7 + pulse * 0.6;\n          continue;\n        }\n\n        if (w.phase === \"out\" || w.phase === \"back\") {\n          w.flyProg = Math.min(1, w.flyProg + dt / FLY_DUR);\n          const k = w.flyProg * w.flyProg * (3 - 2 * w.flyProg);   // smoothstep\n          const a = w.phase === \"out\" ? w.home : w.site;\n          const b = w.phase === \"out\" ? w.site : w.home;\n          w.mesh.position.lerpVectors(a, b, k);\n          ud.glow.material.opacity = 0.3;\n          if (w.flyProg >= 1) {\n            if (w.phase === \"out\") { w.phase = \"work\"; w.timer = WORK_TIME + Math.random() * WORK_JITTER; }\n            else { w.phase = \"done\"; w.mesh.position.copy(w.home); }\n          }\n        } else if (w.phase === \"work\") {\n          w.timer = Math.max(0, w.timer - dt);\n          const near = 1 - Math.min(1, w.timer / WORK_TIME);\n          ud.eyeMat.emissiveIntensity = 1.0 + near * 1.4;\n          ud.glow.material.opacity = 0.22;\n          // welding sparks at the tool tip\n          if (Math.random() < dt * 14) {\n            const tip = ud.tool.getWorldPosition(new THREE.Vector3());\n            spawnSpark(tip, 0xffb86b, 4);\n          }\n          if (w.timer <= 0) {\n            emitSlate(w.jobIdx);\n            spawnSpark(w.mesh.position.clone(), 0x9af0ff, 12);\n            if (w.queue.length) { w.jobIdx = w.queue.shift(); w.timer = WORK_TIME + Math.random() * WORK_JITTER; }\n            else { w.jobIdx = null; w.phase = \"back\"; w.flyProg = 0; }\n          }\n        } else {   // done — parked back home, dim\n          ud.eyeMat.emissiveIntensity = 0.45 + Math.sin(t * 2 + w.home.x) * 0.1;\n          ud.glow.material.opacity = 0.12;\n        }\n      }\n    }"

Fixed — the 6→12 now makes sense because **you** make it happen.

**The new loop:**
- A drone does **one** job per dispatch, flies its checkpoint up the pass, then **flies home and goes idle** (its SEND ▸ cue comes back).
- You **re-send it** (click, or Space sends every idle drone) for its next job. 6 drones you each send twice = 12 records — the count is the direct result of what you did.
- "Send subagents" is now a live verb the whole run: while you're reviewing, drones keep coming home needing to be sent back out. An idle drone sitting unsent = work not happening = the clock keeps bleeding, so there's real pressure to keep them moving.
- Once a drone's done both its jobs, it parks dim.

## Summary

I found the original Three.js drone model from commit **0553cd7** ("Add Level 2 'The Drone Bay'" from 2026-06-10) in `/src/droneBayView.js`.

### Commit & File Location
- **Commit:** `0553cd7` — "Add Level 2 'The Drone Bay' + bird's-eye map; shelve the Archive level"
- **File:** `src/droneBayView.js` (lines approximately 280–295 in that commit)

### Complete Drone-Building Function

```javascript
function buildDrone() {
  const g = new THREE.Group();
  const body = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.OctahedronGeometry(0.7, 0),
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x2c3140, metalness: 0.6, roughness: 0.3, emissive: 0x2a8aa6, emissiveIntensity: 1.0 })
  );
  const ring = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.TorusGeometry(1.0, 0.09, 8, 24),
    new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x6fe3ff, transparent: true, opacity: 0.8 })
  );
  ring.rotation.x = Math.PI / 2;
  g.add(body, ring);
  g.userData = { body, ring };
  return g;
}
```

### Animation Details

The drone had two distinct animation modes:

1. **Idle in Bay:** Subtle bobbing + spinning torus ring
   ```javascript
   d.model.position.y = d.home.y + Math.sin((t + d.bobOff) * 2) * 0.15;
   d.model.userData.ring.rotation.z += dt * 1.2;
   ```

2. **Flying/Returning:** Parabolic arc with fast ring spin
   ```javascript
   d.model.position.y += Math.sin(k * Math.PI) * 3;   // arc over the island
   d.model.userData.ring.rotation.z += dt * 6;
   ```

3. **Working (orbiting job site):** Circular orbit with very fast ring spin
   ```javascript
   d.model.position.set(
     s.anchor.position.x + Math.cos(t * 1.4) * 1.2,
     s.anchor.position.y + 6.5 + Math.sin(t * 2.2) * 0.4,
     s.anchor.position.z + Math.sin(t * 1.4) * 1.2
   );
   d.model.userData.ring.rotation.z += dt * 9;
   ```

**Animation summary:** The spinning cyan torus (`ring`) rotates around the dark metallic octahedron body; rotation speed increases during flight and work. The drone bobs gently in the bay, arcs over terrain en route to jobs, and orbits while working.

```
===== prepare-commit-msg =====
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI hooks
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg "$1" "$2" 2>/dev/null || true; else :; fi

===== commit-msg =====
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI hooks
# Commit-msg hook: strip trailer if no user content (allows aborting empty commits)
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git commit-msg "$1" || true; else printf '%s\n' '[entire] Entire CLI is enabled but not installed or not on PATH. Skipping Entire Git hook; continuing. Installation guide: https://docs.entire.io/cli/installation#installation-methods' >&2 || :; fi

===== post-commit =====
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI hooks
# Post-commit hook: condense session data if commit has Entire-Checkpoint trailer
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git post-commit 2>/dev/null || true; else :; fi

===== pre-push =====
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI hooks
# Pre-push hook: push session logs alongside user's push
# $1 is the remote name (e.g., "origin")
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git pre-push "$1" || true; else :; fi

===== post-rewrite =====
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI hooks
# Post-rewrite hook: remap session linkage after amend/rebase rewrites
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git post-rewrite "$1" 2>/dev/null || true; else :; fi
```

> AGENT

I read through your changes. Here's the honest diagnosis, then what I'd do.

**What you actually built vs. what idea #4 describes — they're different things, and that's the clue.**

Your code adds a *routing* step on the **review** side: after `explain`, the card literally prints `install bay: NAV · NAV BAY`, and you click the NAV bay to install it (wrong bay = −4s). But idea #4 is about the **dispatch** side: choosing *which job to assign to which subagent*.

**Why the routing version isn't hitting:** it's a **matching** task, not a decision. The answer is printed on the card — you just find the button with the same letters. There's no thinking, so it's clerical busywork, and the −4s penalty punishes *misclicks*, which reads as frustration, not challenge. Worse, it quietly turns `explain` from "read what the subagent did" into "scan for the bay keyword" — it hollows out the one thing the level teaches.

**The principle:** real dispatcher games (FTL, 911-dispatch, Mini Metro, Overcooked) aren't fun because you *match* a labeled item to a labeled slot. They're fun because of **triage** — more demand than you can serve, and you decide *what to tackle next*, with consequences for what you ignore. Your #4 instinct is right; the *assignment* is where the decision should live, not the sorting of finished output.

So I'd scrap the routing-match and build the board where the choice actually bites. One fork on how far to take it:

> AGENT

Here's how to play the new Level 2:

**1. Open it** — go to **http://localhost:5174/?view=level2** (the dev server's still running). Press **Space** twice to click through the two briefing lines.

**2. Dispatch (left panel — DISPATCH BOARD).** You'll see failing systems listed, each with a symptom ("core dark") and an **urgency bar**. **Click a row** to send a free drone to fix it. The drone lifts off, flies to the hull, and welds. The launch clock starts on your first click.
- You have **6 drones** (shown as "drones N/6"). Send them to whatever's most urgent.
- Bars climb to **amber → red** the longer a system sits unassigned — and red ones drain your clock faster. That's the decision: **fix the worst first.**
- If every drone's busy, you'll get "all subagents busy — wait for one to return." Drones come back free after each job.

**3. Review (the conveyor pass, center).** When a drone finishes, its work rides up the pass as an ice-blue **checkpoint slate**. **Click the slate** → it runs `entire checkpoint explain` and the card opens showing what the subagent did. **Press Y** (or click **ADD TO SHIP**) to install it — it flies to the hull and a system light turns green.

**4. Win.** Keep juggling: assign drones to failures on the left, clear finished slates on the right. Get **all 12 systems online** before the clock hits 0:00, then **type `entire dispatch`** in the panel and press Enter. Done.

**If you run out of time:** press **R** to retry, **N** for a new game. **B** returns to orbit.

The whole challenge is that triage tension — failures pile up faster than 6 drones can clear them, so you're constantly deciding what's most urgent while also keeping the review pass from backing up.

That's much clearer now. Here's what you'll see and do:

**When you start, look at the top-LEFT** — there's now a red, glowing **⚠ FAILING SYSTEMS** panel that pulses for attention. Each row is a broken system (IGNITION COILS, NAV CORE, …) with a green **SEND ▸** tag.

**To play:**
1. **Click a row** in that red panel → a drone flies off to fix that system. Nothing's on a timer until your first click, so take your time at the start.
2. Each row has a little bar that **fills up the longer you ignore it** (orange → red). Red ones drain your launch clock, so send drones to the worst first. You have 6 drones (the "drones free" count up top of the panel).
3. When a drone finishes, its work rides up the **conveyor in the middle** as a glowing slate. **Click the slate** → it shows what the subagent did → **press Y** to add it to the ship (a light turns green).
4. Repeat until all 12 are green, then type **`entire dispatch`** and Enter.

**I also made it easier to learn:** more time (90s), fewer failures at once (starts with 3), and urgency rises slower — so it's not a firehose while you get the hang of it.

> AGENT

Agreed — let's stop piling on. We've stacked a dispatch board, urgency meters, a conveyor, deliver-to-a-slot, re-sending... that's the overcomplication. Let me strip it to the bone.

**The whole game, one screen — the ship, with a few broken parts you actually recognize. Everything happens *on the part itself*:**

1. A part is broken (🔋 **Battery** dead, flashing). **Tap it** → a subagent flies over and fixes it.
2. It comes back changed → **tap it to `explain`** and see what the subagent did.
3. **Accept** → it lights up green.

**The stake:** a launch clock is ticking. Get every part green before it hits zero, or the ship doesn't make it. That's your "something on the line" — no urgency math, no triage board, just the clock and the pile.

That's **3 taps, all in the same spot** (so it's always clear what's happening and where), and it still teaches the one thing the level is about: you don't ship a subagent's work without looking at it (`explain`), then `entire dispatch` at the end.

**Gone:** the separate board, the conveyor, urgency bars, delivering to slots, re-sending.

**Names** — drop the jargon, keep it to parts a person knows. Something like **6** of these:
🔧 Engine · 🫁 Air · 🔋 Battery · 📡 Radio · 🧭 Steering · 💡 Lights

Two quick checks before I rebuild:
- Is that the right level of simple — tap to fix, tap to see what it did, accept, beat the clock?
- Good with ~6 recognizable parts (I'll wire Level 3 to match)? Or do you want a different/longer list?

> DEVELOPER

and it will still be overcooked?

> AGENT

Yes — but honestly, that depends on one thing, and it's worth being clear about it.

The **Overcooked feeling doesn't come from the mechanics we're cutting** (boards, urgency math, delivery). It comes from **concurrency + tempo**: several things demanding you at once, arriving faster than you can calmly keep up, with a clock breathing down your neck. That part stays.

Here's where the juggle lives in the simple version: at any moment you've got **two kinds of demands competing for your taps** —
- parts that just **broke** (send a subagent), and
- parts that came **back fixed** (stop, look at what it did, accept).

When 3–4 of those are flashing at the same time and more keep popping, you're frantically bouncing between "send that one," "review this one," "ugh another broke" — *that's* the Overcooked. The clock is the "something on the line."

What would kill the Overcooked feel is if it went **one-at-a-time and calm** (fix → wait → review → next). We avoid that purely with **pacing**: parts break in overlapping waves and subagents return at staggered times, so you're always behind by a little. That's a tuning dial, not more mechanics.

So: same frantic juggle, far fewer rules. The simplicity is in *what you do* (tap to send, tap to see, accept); the chaos is in *how much is happening at once*.

Want me to build this version? I'll wire the pacing so you're juggling ~3–4 at a time, keep it to the 6 recognizable parts, and we tune the tempo once you can feel it.

Built and verified. Level 2 is now the stripped-down version we talked about.

**How it plays** (refresh **http://localhost:5174/?view=level2**):
- The ship is an arc of **6 recognizable parts** — 🔧 Engine, 🫁 Air, 🔋 Battery, 📡 Radio, 🧭 Steering, 💡 Lights.
- Parts **break in waves** (flashing red, "▶ CLICK TO FIX"). **Click one** → a subagent flies over and fixes it.
- It comes back changed under ice ("✓ CLICK TO REVIEW"). **Click it** → `entire checkpoint explain` shows what the subagent did → **Y to accept** → it turns green.
- **Launch clock** is the stake — get all 6 green before 0:00, then type `entire dispatch`.

Everything for one part happens **in one spot**, so there's no more "where did that go?" — and the Overcooked juggle is there because breaks overlap with reviews (in testing you'd have 3 broken + 1 waiting to review at once).

Verified the whole loop end-to-end with real clicks, zero errors. It's uncommitted so you can feel it first.

- **Level 3 still uses the old jargon names** (nav core, antenna…) — I left its data untouched so I didn't break it. Worth aligning to the new names later for consistency.
- There's some **dead code** left in the file from the old versions — harmless, I'll clean it up once you're happy with the direction.

> AGENT

I read through the current build end to end. Here's my honest take, not the cheerful version.

## What genuinely works now
- **The clarity problem is actually solved.** Each part has one identity (🔧 Engine, 🔋 Battery…) that you watch travel belt → its own labeled slot. You match by reading a slot label, not decoding a bay code. That was the core "it's going to random things" complaint and it's gone.
- **Explain is gated, not decorative.** `installPart` hard-blocks with "run explain before installing" (line 936). So the teaching beat — `entire checkpoint explain` — can't be skipped to win. Good.
- **The loop reads like a real game.** Dispatch → drone welds → slate rides up → review → drag home → `entire dispatch`. That's a clean Overcooked verb chain.

## What I'd flag honestly

**1. The pressure model is more complicated than the gameplay looks.** There are *three* coupled clock drains — base time, belt backlog (`RAIL_DRAIN`), and urgency (`URGENCY_DRAIN`) — plus a separate board-panic signal. That's the "we're overcomplicating it" feedback you gave me, just relocated into invisible timing math. The player feels the clock lurch and can't tell why. I'd collapse it to **one visible pressure**: parts breaking against the clock. Cut urgency-accelerates-the-clock, or surface it so it's legible.

**2. Explain is gated but not *absorbed*.** You're forced to open the card, but you can match purely off the slot label without reading "what the subagent did." That's fine for flow (Diner Dash doesn't quiz you) — but if the teaching goal is "explain is how you learn what happened," nothing makes it land. That's a design decision worth making on purpose, not by accident.

**3. The file is carrying dead weight.** 1183 lines, still hauling the whole abandoned dispatch-board machinery, `GENERIC_JOBS`, `SYMPTOM_BY_JOB`, plus the unused `#db-board` markup/CSS. Harmless at runtime, but it'll confuse the next session and me. Now that the design is settled, this is the moment to cut it.

**4. Cross-level name split.** L2 says Engine/Battery/Radio; L3 (`launchView.js`) still quizzes on IGNITION COILS/NAV CORE — same parts, two names. A player going L2→L3 gets whiplash.

## My recommendation
The *design* is right — don't touch the loop. I'd spend the next pass on **(1) simplifying the clock to one honest pressure** and **(3) deleting the dead code**, then commit. (2) and (4) are decisions I'd want your call on.

Want me to take a swing at simplifying the pressure model + dead-code cleanup, or do you want to playtest the current build first and tell me if the clock *feels* off before I change it?

  "content": "// CDP smoke test for Level 2 after the pressure-model simplification.\nconst WS = process.argv[2];\nconst ws = new WebSocket(WS);\nlet id = 0;\nconst pending = new Map();\nconst exceptions = [];\nconst consoleErrors = [];\n\nfunction send(method, params = {}) {\n  return new Promise((res) => { const i = ++id; pending.set(i, res); ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id: i, method, params })); });\n}\nconst sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));\n\nws.onmessage = (m) => {\n  const msg = JSON.parse(m.data);\n  if (msg.id && pending.has(msg.id)) { pending.get(msg.id)(msg.result); pending.delete(msg.id); return; }\n  if (msg.method === \"Runtime.exceptionThrown\") {\n    exceptions.push(msg.params.exceptionDetails.exception?.description || msg.params.exceptionDetails.text);\n  }\n  if (msg.method === \"Runtime.consoleAPICalled\" && msg.params.type === \"error\") {\n    consoleErrors.push(msg.params.args.map((a) => a.value || a.description).join(\" \"));\n  }\n};\n\nasync function evalJs(expr) {\n  const r = await send(\"Runtime.evaluate\", { expression: expr, returnByValue: true });\n  return r.result?.value;\n}\nasync function clickAt(x, y) {\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchMouseEvent\", { type: \"mousePressed\", x, y, button: \"left\", clickCount: 1 });\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchMouseEvent\", { type: \"mouseReleased\", x, y, button: \"left\", clickCount: 1 });\n}\nasync function key(code, k) {\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchKeyEvent\", { type: \"keyDown\", code, key: k, windowsVirtualKeyCode: code === \"Space\" ? 32 : 13 });\n  await send(\"Input.dispatchKeyEvent\", { type: \"keyUp\", code, key: k, windowsVirtualKeyCode: code === \"Space\" ? 32 : 13 });\n}\n\nws.onopen = async () => {\n  await send(\"Runtime.enable\");\n  await send(\"Page.enable\");\n  await sleep(1500);\n\n  // advance briefing to start\n  await key(\"Space\", \" \"); await sleep(250);\n  await key(\"Space\", \" \"); await sleep(250);\n  await key(\"Enter\", \"Enter\"); await sleep(800);\n\n  const started = await evalJs(`!!document.getElementById('db-board') && !document.getElementById('db-board').classList.contains('hidden')`);\n\n  // click every broken board dot we can find (DOM buttons), dispatching subagents\n  let dispatched = 0;\n  for (let pass = 0; pass < 8; pass++) {\n    const rects = await evalJs(`(()=>{const b=[...document.querySelectorAll('.db-board-dot.is-broken:not([disabled])')];return b.map(e=>{const r=e.getBoundingClientRect();return {x:r.x+r.width/2,y:r.y+r.height/2}})})()`);\n    for (const r of rects || []) { await clickAt(r.x, r.y); await sleep(120); dispatched++; }\n    await sleep(900);\n  }\n\n  // let the loop run while blocks pile up unreviewed (exercises new drain + panic)\n  await sleep(4000);\n\n  const tally = await evalJs(`document.getElementById('db-systems-rows')?.innerText || ''`);\n  const clock = await evalJs(`document.getElementById('db-countdown-time')?.innerText || ''`);\n  const skyR = await evalJs(`(()=>{const c=document.querySelector('canvas');return 'sky-ok'})()`);\n\n  // screenshot\n  const shot = await send(\"Page.captureScreenshot\", { format: \"png\" });\n  if (shot?.data) (await import(\"fs\")).writeFileSync(\"/tmp/l2_smoke.png\", Buffer.from(shot.data, \"base64\"));\n\n  console.log(JSON.stringify({\n    started, dispatched, clock,\n    tally: tally.replace(/\\s+/g, \" \").trim(),\n    exceptions, consoleErrors,\n  }, null, 2));\n  ws.close();\n  process.exit(0);\n};\nws.onerror = (e) => { console.error(\"WS error\", e.message); process.exit(1); };\n"
}

10	Agreed with Rizel 2026-06-10, replacing the built Archive level (shelved, kept in `src/archiveView.js`, playable at `?view=archive`). BUILT 2026-06-10 in `src/droneBayView.js` (#db-hud markup, post-L1 pin + ?view=level2 route here now); 150s clock, 18s drone work time, both tunable. Drones IMPROVISE (Rizel's "bow turns into a sword"): coils→Plasma Ring, nav core→Star Dome, dish→Signal Spire, scrubbers→Garden Pod, struts→Grav Skid — the transformation creates the "what did you DO?" urge that explain satisfies. Beam-color status grammar: amber broken → cyan working → ice-blue review-me → none (upgrade is the landmark). Ground levels in the day-to-day agentic workflow: **delegate → review → accept**. Level 2 "The Drone Bay": 5 broken ship systems (ignition coils, nav core, antenna, life support, landing struts), 5 drones (one per job, no economy). Assign with E (drone flies out and works); player chooses serial vs. parallel — the one countdown makes parallel the rational move. Finished sites seal under a checkpoint; walk up → terminal opens **pre-filled** with `entire checkpoint explain <id>` (Rizel: never type ids) → Enter → story card of what the drone did → **ADD TO SHIP** confirm (Y) → meter +20%. Finish line (changed 2026-06-10): the FIFTH accept keeps the terminal open and you type `entire dispatch` right there — the day's report writes itself from the checkpoints ("Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" per the real CLI). Rizel couldn't find the end-of-level console ("where am I supposed to be going") → no final fetch-quest; next command at the prompt you're already at. `entire checkpoint list` still accepted as an optional L1 callback. Bird's-eye map (M, src/overhead.js) added to all island levels; terminals stay open over it. Deliberately excluded: botched-drone deduction puzzles, drone management, extracting values from explanations (Rizel rejected those as "too complicated"). Teaching — use Rizel's framing (2026-06-10), not workflow jargon like "delegate→review→accept": the level shows **multiple agents working in parallel, seeing what work each did (explain), and getting a summary at the end (dispatch)**. Sending a drone is one button (spectacle, not a lesson); ADD TO SHIP is just the gate that makes reading the explanation non-skippable. Terminology (Rizel, 2026-06-10): in all player-facing copy the workers are called **subagents**, never drones — only the location keeps the name "The Drone Bay" (possible later rename; candidates discussed: The Fleet, Mission Control, fiction-patch "drones piloted by subagents"). Why: the word should make the real-world mapping unmistakable — these are agents working in parallel (or sequentially, player's choice) and you get insight into their work. Not metaphor decoration. See [[level2-archive-search-design]] and [[level2-design-direction]].
11	
12	**REWORKED 2026-06-16 — starting-grid / mission-control rebuild.** Rizel disliked walking the island to scattered sites; redesigned the dispatch layer (NOT the explain/dispatch teaching, which is unchanged) into a fixed-camera racing-grid. droneBayView.js rewritten: dropped first-person (firstPerson.js), overhead map (overhead.js), pointer-lock, walk-up proximity, and the E-assign key. Now: fixed camera over 5 parallel lanes; subagents are **cars** (not drones) parked on a grid, rails drawn along terrain. **Click a car = arm; Space = green flag (launches all armed at once); click a moving car = nitro boost.** This one mechanic gives both sequential (arm-one-then-Space) and parallel (arm all five) — Rizel explicitly wanted both. Nitro = the engagement-during-travel + catch-up tool (3 charges/run, shown as dots in #db-systems-rows); Rizel didn't care what "powerups" meant, "just something where they go faster." Lanes are LOCAL to L2 (props placed at lane-ends, START_Z=64→FINISH_Z=-34, slight fan) and decoupled from SYSTEMS.pos — left SYSTEMS.pos untouched because launchView.js (L3) still reads it for its own island. Tunables: BASE_SPEED 1/14, BOOST_MULT 2.6, BOOST_DUR 2.2, NITRO_MAX 3, TOTAL_TIME 150. Kept: clock+panic sky, checkpoint cards, click-sealed-car→pre-filled explain→ADD TO SHIP→dispatch finish, win/fail. Open/untested live: car speed feel, whether any lane-end finish lands in water. Briefing + CONTROLS in index.html (#db-briefing) rewritten to match (click/Space, no WASD/E/M).
13	
14	**TENSION REBUILD 2026-06-16 — dispatch grid (drag + generic hazards).** Playtest of the starting-grid version: "kinda good but no tension." Diagnosed: cars were already on rails (just flipping a switch), clock far too generous (150s vs ~14s parallel), nitro had no job, parallel overlap means the slowest lane sets finish time so an aggregate clock CAN'T create parallel tension (mathematically — boosting only the slowest barely helps). Conclusion: parallel "chaos" tension MUST come from a per-lane failure stake, not the clock. Agreed direction with Rizel: **true drag + generic hazards** (rejected specialty-matching cars/Decoder/Repair — it's the "drone management" she already killed, blows the 15s onboarding, and telegraphs outcomes which guts the explain payoff). Built in droneBayView.js: cars now wait in a BAY (BAY_Z=START_Z+26=90), tracks start EMPTY. ## What I changed

**1. Collapsed the pressure model to one honest, visible signal.**
The clock used to drain from *three* coupled sources you couldn't see — a per-part urgency meter, urgency-accelerates-the-clock, and belt-backlog — plus board urgency rings. That's the hidden complexity behind the "we're overcomplicating it" feeling.

Now: **the clock ticks at 1×, and the only thing that speeds it up is sealed blocks on the belt** — work you haven't run `explain` on yet:
```js
const drain = dt * (1 + SEAL_DRAIN * unreviewedCount());
```
I deliberately tied it to *unreviewed* blocks, not all blocks — so **running `explain` is what relieves the pressure**. That makes the lesson the release valve, and you can literally *see* the pile that's hurting you. The panic sky reddens off the same number. Urgency meters/rings are gone entirely.

**2. Deleted the dead code.** `GENERIC_JOBS`, `JOBS`, and the unused `buildShipBoard` 3D helper, plus the orphaned urgency CSS. `droneBayView.js` went ~1250 → 1070 lines. Kept the strut/grav-skid builders and the `SYSTEMS`/`UPGRADE_BUILDERS` exports since L3 imports them.

one of the boring parts of this is that the matching will always be in order

> AGENT

Good catch — that's the real flaw. Parts break in a fixed order (`[0,1.5,4,...]` always Engine→Air→Battery→…), get dispatched in that order, return in that order, and the slots are laid out left-to-right in that same order. So the leftmost belt slate always belongs to the leftmost slot — you never actually read a label, you just drag straight up. That's not matching, it's a conveyor.

The fix: make the slate's destination *not* line up with where it arrives. I'll shuffle both the **slot layout** (which part sits at which spot) and the **break order**, re-rolled each run — so you always have to read the label and route it, Overcooked-style. Let me find the exact spots.

> AGENT

Fixed. You were right — it was a conveyor, not a matching game.

**What was happening:** parts broke in a fixed order (Engine→Air→Battery→…), so they got dispatched in order, returned in order, and the slots were laid out left-to-right in that *same* order. The leftmost slate always belonged to the leftmost slot → you'd just drag straight up without ever reading a label.

**The fix:** each run now re-rolls two things with a Fisher-Yates shuffle:
- **Slot layout** — which spot along the hull each part occupies (the screenshot now reads Battery · Steering · Lights · Air · Radio · Engine, not index order)
- **Break order** — which part fails when

So a slate riding up the belt never lines up under its destination — you have to read the 🔧/🔋/📡 label and route it across the hull, and it's different every retry. That's the actual Diner-Dash "find where the soup goes" lookup. Re-rolls on reset too, so retries stay fresh.

Verified headless: shuffled labels render, full loop runs, zero exceptions. Still uncommitted so you can feel it.

One thing worth noting while you play: the labels are now doing all the work, which makes **open question #2 less of a worry** (you're forced to read the slate to route it) but raises the stakes on readability — if the icons/names are hard to scan quickly under time pressure, that'll show up now. Tell me how the routing feels.

> DEVELOPER

i think it should be that some things take longer to fix than others

> AGENT

Good idea — right now every fix takes the same ~4s plus random jitter, so the belt fills evenly and there's no reason to think about *which* subagent to send first. Making it a property of the part adds real texture: a big Engine rebuild keeps a subagent out a long time, Lights comes back fast. Let me wire fix time into each part.

So if you dispatch the slow jobs first they're working while you handle the quick ones, versus dumping everything and watching three slates land at once. It rewards thinking about *order* of dispatch, which there was zero reason to do before.

Mostly yes — I agree with the direction, with one guardrail. Let me be specific about what I'm agreeing to and the one trap to avoid.

**Where I agree:**
- **Splitting dispatch from matching is right.** Right now the ship slot does triple duty — it's the broken alarm, the dispatch button, *and* the drag target. That overload is muddy, and it's also why we have two redundant dispatch surfaces (the board *and* the slots). Giving "send help" and "put it home" their own surfaces is cleaner.
- **The board needs simplifying** — agreed, it's a tacked-on HTML panel right now, not a designed thing.
- **Redoing the visuals of both** — agreed.

**The one guardrail (this is the whole ballgame):** keep it to **two zones, not three.** The thing that killed the old triage build was a part's life scattered across board → drone → belt → pip — four places to babysit. Your loop is healthier *if* it reads as one flow with two ends:

- **Top = dispatch board:** what's broken, click to send. Nothing else.
- **Bottom = belt → matching squares:** what came back, drag it home.

Two halves of one loop, not three separate things to watch. If we hold that line, I think your version is *better* than what's there now.

**Two things I'd insist we keep:**
1. **Drop the 3D-slot-as-dispatch entirely** so there's exactly *one* way to send a subagent (the board). Otherwise the redundancy survives the redesign.
2. **Matching squares stay labeled + shuffled** — that's the read-the-label routing we just added. Don't lose it, or we're back to a conveyor.

One honest note: separating them means the broken alarm (board) and the part's home (square) live in different places, so the eye has to learn "Engine alert up top → Engine square down there." That's fine — it's exactly how Overcooked's order tickets and serving windows work — but it's *why* the labels have to be crisp.

Yeah, I agree — and I actually like it more than the labeled board. Here's why it works: it splits the game into a **dumb half and a smart half.** Dispatch becomes pure reflex — "red dot appeared, send a subagent, keep up" — no reading, no decisions. All the *thinking* moves to the matching side, where it belongs. That's a cleaner split than what we have.

It also sets up something we've been missing. Follow the logic: if the board doesn't tell you what's broken, then **the only way to find out what a subagent actually fixed is to run `explain` on what comes back.** Right now the slate rides up already labeled "🔧 Engine," so explain is skippable — you can match off the label. But if the returned work comes back **sealed and anonymous**, then:

> red dot → send → a sealed mystery block rides up → **`explain` reveals "this is the Engine fix"** → *now* you can match it to the Engine square.

That makes explain finally load-bearing — you literally can't route it without reading it. Which is the actual lesson of the level. It's also exactly the Diner-Dash beat: the order's a mystery until you check the ticket, *then* you know where it goes.

So my question back: **do you want the returned work sealed/anonymous until you explain it?** That's the natural payoff of anonymous dispatch, and it's the thing that justifies explain existing at all. (If yes, the loop is: dots → send → sealed block → explain to reveal → drag to its square.)

One small heads-up, since it touches what you asked last time: if the dots are anonymous, you **can't pick the slow Engine to send first** — you don't know which dot is which. The variable fix times still make the belt arrive all staggered and messy (good), you just can't strategize *at dispatch*. I think that's fine and more honest — you don't know how bad a failure is until the subagent gets in there — but flagging it in case "send the slow ones first" was part of the appeal for you.

Built and verified. Here's what changed:

**The board is now just anonymous red dots** — no "Battery," no labels, no letters. One red dot per failure. Click it, a subagent flies. That's the whole "dumb half": pure reflex, keep up with the dots.

**Dispatch moved entirely off the ship.** The hull squares no longer turn red or act as dispatch buttons — they're pure labeled destinations now (that also kills the old two-dispatch-surfaces redundancy you flagged). The hull stays calm and reveals *nothing* about what's broken.

**Returned work comes back sealed.** A subagent's finished block rides up the belt as a featureless ice block — you can't tell what it is. Running **`entire checkpoint explain`** is now the *only* way to find out: it cracks the seal, reveals "🔧 Engine," and *then* you can read it and drag it to the matching square. So explain is finally load-bearing — you literally can't route a block without it. That's the Diner-Dash beat: the ticket's a mystery until you check it.

The full loop now:
> anonymous red dot → click to send → **sealed mystery block** rides up → click to **explain** (reveals what it is) → drag to its matching labeled square → all 6 → `entire dispatch`

Verified headless: dots have zero labels, hull squares neutral, belt blocks sealed, zero exceptions. Screenshot confirmed it reads exactly like the split you described.

Two notes from the build:
- I kept the matching squares as **the ship hull** (not a separate abstract grid) — preserves the "repairing the actual ship" feel. Easy to switch if you'd rather have a distinct grid.
- The matching squares deliberately **don't glow** until you're dragging onto them — so you genuinely have to read the revealed block and find its square, not just chase a highlight. If that feels too unguided in play, I can add a subtle target hint.

It's uncommitted — play it and tell me how the sealed→explain→match rhythm feels.

}

break; }\n      }\n    }\n    await sleep(800);\n  }\n  await sleep(3000);\n  const after = await ev(`document.getElementById('db-systems-rows')?.innerText.replace(/\\\\s+/g,' ').trim()`);\n  const boardHidden = await ev(`document.getElementById('db-board')?.classList.contains('hidden')`);\n  const shot = await send(\"Page.captureScreenshot\", { format: \"png\" });\n  if (shot?.data) (await import(\"fs\")).writeFileSync(\"/tmp/l2_3d.png\", Buffer.from(shot.data, \"base64\"));\n  console.log(JSON.stringify({ before, after, dispatched, boardHidden, exceptions, consoleErrors }, null, 2));\n  ws.close(); What it brings back rides up the belt, sealed.\", 8000);\n  }"
}

> AGENT

Done. The board now starts **full of six little red dots**, and they're pure job markers — clicking one pulls the next repair from a shuffled queue, so the dot you click never hints at which sealed block comes back. You still only find out by running `explain`.

One thing that changed as a consequence, worth knowing before you play: since all the dots are there at once (no more staggered "breaking"), **dispatch is now a quick opening burst** — click the six dots, six subagents fly out — and the actual game becomes keeping up with the *returns*: blocks come back at different times (the 2.5–7.5s fix times), you explain each, and race to match them before the clock + sealed-backlog drain catches you.

If that opening burst feels too frontloaded (everyone leaves at once), I can stagger it back a bit — e.g., only N dots clickable at first with more appearing, or cap how many subagents are free early. But that's a pacing call best made by feel.

Verified clean, uncommitted. Give it a play.

  "new_string": "  // grade the placements: correct ones lock in green (✓); wrong ones flash and\n  // ride back out on the belt to be re-matched. Win only when all are correct.\n  function gradeAndDispatch() {\n    const wrong = parts.filter((p) => p.state === \"placed\" && p.placedIn !== p.idx);\n    if (wrong.length) {\n      for (const p of wrong) {\n        const sq = parts[p.placedIn];\n        sq.userData ? null : null;\n        sq.slot.userData.holder.remove(p.slateMesh);\n        scene.add(p.slateMesh);\n        p.slateMesh.scale.setScalar(1);\n        spawnSpark(sq.slotPos.clone(), 0xff3b2e, 14);\n        p.state = \"review\"; p.placedIn = null; p.beltX = ENTRANCE_X;\n        p.slateMesh.position.set(ENTRANCE_X, BELT_Y, 2);\n        belted.push(p.idx);\n      }\n      panelMode = null; buffer = \"\"; closePanel(); updateSystems();\n      flashTerminal(`✗ ${wrong.length} in the wrong bay — they're back on the belt; re-match and dispatch again`, false);\n      showTutorial(`${wrong.length} block(s) were in the wrong bay — back on the belt. Fix the matches, then run \\`entire dispatch\\` again.`, 7000);\n      return;\n    }\n    // all correct → lock in (✓) and finish\n    for (const p of parts) {\n      if (p.state === \"placed\") { p.state = \"online\"; p.installT = PART_MELT; spawnSpark(p.slot.position.clone(), 0x7cffb0, 14); }\n    }\n    updateSystems();\n    sendDispatch();\n  }\n  function submitCommand() {\n    const n = normalizeCmd(buffer); buffer = \"\";\n    if (!n) { renderPanel(); return; }\n    if (/^entire dispatch$/.test(n)) { gradeAndDispatch(); return; }"

**What changed:**
- The green "DROP HERE" glow is **gone** — squares never light up to point you at the answer.
- You **drop a block into any bay** and it stays put (the bay glows a neutral amber, "placed but unconfirmed").
